narrative:
The model predicted a 60.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

Three pieces of information about you drove that decision, ranked by importance. First, your family's upper-middle income bracket pushed the prediction toward failure. While this is the most common income group among accepted students (45%), the model sees it as a risk factor that slightly increases the chance of not passing the bar. 

Second, your strong performance in your third year of law school worked in your favor. Being in the top decile far exceeds the average of accepted students (around 5.8), and this achievement pulled the prediction noticeably toward passing.

Third, your LSAT score of 45 also increased the chance of failure. Although this score is well above the average of 37 for accepted students, the model weighed it as a factor that slightly raised the risk of not passing on the first try.

In short, your excellent third-year grades helped your case, but your family income category and LSAT score outweighed that positive signal enough to push the overall risk above the limit.

What you should do next is retake the LSAT and aim for an even higher score, or consider strengthening other parts of your profile before reapplying. Many students improve their outcomes this way. (218 words)
